paras: The threatened lynching of Bart Philips took place in Woodstock, Shenandoah County, Virginia, on the night of June 6, 1881, when a party of citizens formed to hang Philips, a Black man suspected of setting fire to the stables behind Welsh's Hotel. Philips was kept out of the crowd's reach, quietly arrested and committed to jail to await indictment.

At about 10 o'clock on a Monday night, fire destroyed the two large stables in the rear of Welsh's Hotel, together with farm implements and about five thousand shingles. Several men were hurt fighting the fire, among them Lieut. Gatewood, who was burned about the face.

The Shenandoah Herald wrote that the fire was "the work of an incendiary" and that Philips, described as "a negro," had been seen near the stables acting in a "very suspicious" manner. As soon as the fire was out, a party was formed "for the purpose of hanging Philips." According to the Herald, Philips owed his life to "fortunate circumstances" that kept him away from the "enfiuriated crowd of citizens," and he was then quietly arrested and jailed under precautions to secure him.

On June 7 Philips was brought before Justice Rodeffer and committed for indictment. At the June county court term a special grand jury indicted a "Wm. B. Phillips alias Wm. B. Brown" for an unnamed felony, but the report does not connect the case to the fire. No report of a trial or of any action against the men who sought to hang Philips appears in the coverage.

The Woodstock-based Shenandoah Herald reported it on June 8 under the heading "FIRE.", near the end of a long account of the blaze. The Herald stated as its own judgment that "strong circumstantial evidence indicated his guilt" and described the crowd's "indignation" without criticizing it. On June 21 the Staunton Spectator ran a shorter item, "Stables Burned in Woodstock," that follows the Herald closely and adds that "threats of Lynching him were made." No account from Philips or from any Black source appears in the coverage.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Bart Philips
bases: A party of citizens formed to hang a Black man suspected of setting a stable fire, but he was kept out of its reach and jailed (A1, A2).

A 'party' and an 'enfiuriated crowd of citizens' sought to hang Philips on suspicion of arson, which meets the group and pretext elements, but no one was killed; it was a threatened lynching (A1, A2).
Two papers carried the story, but the Staunton Spectator's item repeats the Shenandoah Herald's details nearly word for word and appears drawn from it, so there is one independent account (A1, A2).

accounts.label: Woodstock local paper
accounts.gist: The Shenandoah Herald said an incendiary fired the stables, that Philips was seen nearby acting suspiciously, and that a party formed to hang him; 'fortunate circumstances' kept him from the crowd until he was quietly jailed.

accounts.label: Staunton regional paper
accounts.gist: The Staunton Spectator, two weeks later, said Phillips was suspected, arrested and committed to await a grand jury, and that 'threats of Lynching him were made'.

framing.detail: Headed 'FIRE.', the Herald item put the hanging party within a fire report, called the citizens 'enfiuriated', and stated that 'strong circumstantial evidence indicated his guilt' without condemning the mob.
The Staunton Spectator ran 'Stables Burned in Woodstock' as a regional brief noting 'the excitement against him was great' and the lynching threats.

record_check.dossier: Woodstock: the Woodstock-based Shenandoah Herald placed Welsh's Hotel 'in this place', and the Staunton Spectator headed its item 'Stables Burned in Woodstock'.
Bart Philips (A1); spelled Bart Phillips in A2

record_check.record: He was hidden from the crowd, arrested quietly and committed to jail.
record_check.dossier: The Herald says 'fortunate circumstances' kept him out of the crowd's reach; it does not say he was hidden. He was brought before Justice Rodeffer and committed for indictment.
Two white papers carried the episode (Shenandoah Herald, Staunton Spectator).

info: Monday night, about 10 o'clock (June 6, 1881, by the Herald's 'last Monday' in its June 8 issue)
Stables in the rear of Welsh's Hotel, Woodstock
Bart Philips (Phillips in A2), described as 'a negro'
Suspected of setting the fire that burned the hotel stables; the Herald said 'strong circumstantial evidence indicated his guilt'
A 'party' formed after the fire; 'crowd of citizens'
Felony cases of the June term were continued to the next term; no trial report found

sources.note: Local report: stables behind Welsh's Hotel 'in this place' fired Monday night; Bart Philips, 'a negro', suspected; a party formed to hang him; arrested, jailed, committed for indictment by Justice Rodeffer.
quotes: A negro by the name of Bart Philips was seen in the neighborhood of the stables and his conduct was very suspicious.
As soon as the fire was subdued a party was formed for the purpose of hanging Philips.
Philips owes his life to the fortunate circumstances that kept him out of the reach of the enfiuriated crowd of citizens.
He was quietly arrested and committed to jail, and every precaution necessary to secure him was taken.
